questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Mosquitoes and dengue spreading as it warms
Why young children often get high fevers
How to protect your house from insects
The history of malaria in Africa and Asia
questions.why: They look at mosquitoes spreading to new areas with warming temperatures, and the disease dengue.

questions.q: How many people do mosquito-borne diseases kill each year?
options: About 150,000
About one million children
Around three-quarters of a million
About five million
questions.why: Neil says they kill around three-quarters of a million people globally every year.

questions.q: According to Dr Dewi Iriani, when might a doctor suspect dengue?
options: When a patient has only muscle aches and pains
When a patient has a bad cough for a week
When a child can't sleep because of the heat
When fever comes with red spots or lasts 3 days
questions.why: She says red spots on the skin or a fever lasting three days suggest dengue.

questions.q: What problem does Dr Iriani describe with parents?
options: They don't know the critical days, so come late
They refuse to take their children to hospital
They give children the wrong kind of medicine
They can't afford to pay for hospital treatment
questions.why: She says parents don't know about the critical window, and by the time they come it's difficult to help.

questions.q: How does drought help mosquitoes breed?
options: It makes the air much hotter at night
People store water in buckets, where they breed
It kills the birds and fish that eat mosquitoes
It makes rivers flood after the rain
questions.why: Drought forces people to collect drinking water in buckets, giving mosquitoes places to breed.

questions.q: According to Professor Manisha Kulkarni, what happens at higher temperatures?
options: Mosquitoes die much more quickly in the heat
Mosquitoes bite people much less often
The virus copies itself faster in the mosquito
The virus becomes weaker and less dangerous
questions.why: She says the higher the temperature, the quicker the mosquito can replicate the virus.

questions.q: Why does Paul Conolly mention poverty?
options: To say it has nothing to do with dengue
To explain why vaccines are so expensive
To show why dengue is rare in big cities
Crowded, poor city life exposes more people
questions.why: He says as people move to cramped cities with poor sanitation, more are exposed to dengue.

questions.q: What good news does Neil mention at the end?
options: Mosquitoes are leaving Europe
Early warning systems and work on a vaccine
Dengue cases in Indonesia have fallen
Climate change has slowed down
questions.why: He mentions early warning systems that predict outbreaks and ongoing work to produce a vaccine.
